as_told: In 1981 a strange arcade game called Polybius appeared in a few arcades near Portland, Oregon. Players suffered amnesia, nightmares and seizures, and men in black coats came to collect data from the machines rather than coins. The game was a secret government (CIA or military) experiment in mind control, and the machines vanished after about a month.
lesson: Governments secretly run mind experiments on unsuspecting members of the public.
what_happened: The first known telling is an anonymous entry on the arcade database coinop.org, last modified on 6 February 2000 with the note 'New addition - anyone heard of this game?'. It claims a ROM of the game had turned up, but the site never published it; its 2009 update still promised new information. My searches (Open Library full text and web searches) found no record of Polybius from 1981; I could not search 1981 newspapers or coin-op trade magazines.
false_part: No record shows that a game called Polybius existed in 1981 or that any government used an arcade game for mind experiments.

earliest_telling.who: Anonymous contributor to coinop.org (The Clickto Network)
earliest_telling.where: coinop.org game page 'Polybius' (Wayback copy of 3 March 2000)
earliest_telling.quote: used some kind of proprietary behavior modification algorithms developed for the CIA or something

lesson_verdict.why: A 1977 US Senate hearing records that the CIA's MKULTRA program tested drugs, including LSD, on citizens who did not know they were being tested; the hearing records that the testing was later stopped. Nothing in it concerns video games, so it supports the general lesson but not this story.

source.what: Project MKULTRA, the CIA's Program of Research in Behavioral Modification: Joint Hearing before the Select Committee on Intelligence and the Subcommittee on Health and Scientific Research, US Senate, 3 August 1977 (statement of Senator Edward Kennedy)
source.quote: covert drug tests on unwitting citizens “at all social levels, high and low, native Americans and foreign.”

search_steps: Open Library full-text search for Polybius arcade Portland and for Sinnesloschen: no hit about the game before 2000.

Read the English Wikipedia article as a lead: it cites the coinop.org page (Wayback, 3 March 2000), a 2019-2020 version of it, Skeptoid episode 362 and Oregonian and Register-Guard articles of 1981-1982, and says no archived Usenet posts discuss Polybius.

Saved the coinop.org page from the Wayback Machine (capture 3 March 2000; 'Last Modification of this game: 2/6/2000 10:23:41 AM'). Its date of 1998 shown in later versions is said by leads to be a system default; I could not check that.

Saved the 2020 Wayback copy of the coinop.org page to look for a correction by the teller: the text is unchanged, with a 2009 update ('one of us is flying to the Kyiv, Ukraine area tomorrow') and no retraction.

Read Skeptoid episode 362 (Brian Dunning) as a lead: it cites the Eugene Register-Guard, 29 November 1981, 'Tummy Derails Asteroids Champ' (AP), and The Oregonian, 9 December 1981, 'Video Games Gambling Count Admitted'. The Register-Guard page is a scanned image in Google News Archive and The Oregonian is behind a paywall, so I did not save or quote them.
Usenet: a web search for Polybius on Google Groups found no dated post; secondary accounts mention a 2000 Usenet repost and a claimed 1994 post, neither found.
Chronicling America (blocked by a browser check) does not cover 1981 in any case; Google Books quota was exceeded.
Lesson: the US Senate's own copy of the 1977 MKULTRA hearing returned 403; I did not retry and saved an archive.org copy of the printed hearing instead.
confidence_note: The rules require positive evidence for 'invented', and I found only the absence of any 1981 record, so the class is 'unsupported'; most researchers treat the game as a hoax. Who wrote the coinop.org entry is unknown. The 1981 Portland newspaper reports that leads cite were not read.
